46:12.text: And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the LORD, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.

provenance.other: “Fight for your brethren” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 4:14, and the list that follows it — “your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses” — is likewise unique to that verse. The Book of Mormon's list is shorter and the pronouns are first-person plural: “our God, our religion, and freedom, and our peace, our wives, and our children.”
provenance.alternative: “Our wives and our children” with the Book of Mormon's own pronoun occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 14:3 — but there the phrase belongs to the wilderness generation arguing for surrender, which is the opposite of a muster cry. See the exclusion register at this verse.
provenance.significance: Nehemiah 4 is the King James Bible's one scene of a civil population arming itself around a leader who has just rallied it by naming what it stands to lose, and it is the chapter in which the workers build with a weapon in one hand and a trumpeter beside the leader (4:17-20). Moroni's rent coat on a pole is that trumpet: an improvised signal raised over a people who must be told, in a list, what they are defending. Recover Nehemiah's context and the borrowing supplies what Alma 46 never says outright — that the title of liberty is a wall-building banner, defensive and domestic, not a conquest standard. Nehemiah's rally ends “our God shall fight for us” (4:20); Moroni's ends with a prayer that God will favour the cause.

46:12.note: The writing on the rent coat is a list of goods in the possessive plural — God, religion, freedom, peace, wives, children — and the KJV has one such list on the lips of one such leader, at Nehemiah 4:14, where it is likewise preceded by a call to remember. Moroni writes “In memory of our God”; Nehemiah says “remember the LORD.” No clause is reproduced, and the case rests on the shape of the sentence and the identity of the scene rather than on shared wording; catalogued as an allusion at moderate confidence for that reason. It falls far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is in no sense a quotation.
46:12.whyNot: Every content word in Moroni's list is ordinary, the pronouns differ from Nehemiah's, and the last two items in the KJV list (daughters, houses) are absent. A leader listing wives and children as what an army defends is not a literary borrowing on its own; only Nehemiah 4's whole situation makes the case.

46:12.text: And Ahijah caught the new garment that was on him, and rent it in twelve pieces:

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 15:27-28 and 1 Kings 11:30-31 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Hath rent the kingdom” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Samuel 15:28 and 28:17, both of Saul; 1 Kings 11:31 has the cognate “I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon.” These are the Bible's two rent-garment political signs.
provenance.significance: The Bible tears a garment twice as an act of state, and both times the tearing announces that a kingdom is being taken away from a man who wanted to keep it: Samuel's mantle rent as Saul clutches it, Ahijah's new garment rent into twelve pieces for Jeroboam. Alma 46 inverts the figure precisely. Amalickiah is a man who wants to be king (46:4), and the garment torn against him is torn not by a prophet but by a commander, and not into a kingdom's portions but into a single banner. The type-scene's grammar is preserved and its outcome reversed: the rending here does not transfer a monarchy, it abolishes the claim to one.

46:12.note: Moroni rends his coat, takes a piece of it, and raises it on a pole as a public sign against a would-be king. There is almost no shared wording — the case is entirely at the level of the scene — and it is catalogued as figural for that reason. What makes it more than a coincidence of gesture is 46:21, where the covenant reads the sign the way 1 Samuel 15:28 reads Samuel's mantle: the tearing is a declaration of what God will do to the tearer's own party if it transgresses. Compare Hays on the recovery of a precursor's context; the argument here is that the Book of Mormon has borrowed the biblical logic of the torn garment rather than any biblical sentence.
46:12.whyNot: Rending a garment is the commonest gesture of grief and outrage in the KJV — “rent his clothes” alone occurs in fifteen verses — and Moroni's tearing may be nothing but that. Neither 1 Samuel 15 nor 1 Kings 11 supplies a phrase, and a reader who declines the type-scene is left with no evidence at all.

46:13.text: Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness;

provenance.other: “The whole armour” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ephesians 6:11 and 6:13; “girt about” in exactly two, Ephesians 6:14 and Revelation 1:13. The 1830 spells the noun “armour” with the KJV's u, which 1920 Americanized to “armor” — the borrowing is plainer in the first edition than in the modern text.
provenance.significance: Paul's panoply is the King James Bible's one catalogue of armour piece by piece, and it is a catalogue of things that are not armour: truth, righteousness, faith, salvation. Alma 46:13 re-literalizes it. Moroni puts on the helmet, the breastplate, the shield and the girded loins as actual metal, and then does with them what Ephesians 6:18 tells the armoured man to do next — “praying always” — bowing to the earth and praying mightily. The chapter then completes the circuit at 46:21, where the people come with their armours girded about their loins to enter a covenant. A figure Paul made spiritual has been made military again, and the prayer that follows the arming is the seam where the two readings meet.

46:13.note: Head-plate, breast-plate, shields, and armour girded about the loins: four pieces, and the same four Ephesians 6 names, in a book whose prophets elsewhere quote that passage's fiery darts. The wording is not Paul's — “head-plate” is not the KJV's helmet and no clause is reproduced — so this is an allusion at moderate confidence, resting on the closed set of items plus the immediate turn to prayer. Below Skousen's threshold by a wide margin.
46:13.whyNot: A soldier arming himself will put on a helmet, a breastplate and a shield whatever his author has read, and 1 Samuel 17:5-6 arms Goliath from the same inventory without any Pauline help. The girded loins are the only item that is more natural as a borrowing than as observation.

46:15.text: And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.

provenance.other: “Christians” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 11:26. The singular “Christian” occurs in two more, Acts 26:28 and 1 Peter 4:16 — three verses in the whole Bible, and Alma 46 draws on all three within nine verses (46:13, 46:15, 46:18, 46:21).
provenance.significance: Acts 11:26 does not say the disciples took the name; it says they were called it, by outsiders, in a city where they were a minority. Alma 46:14-15 reproduces that exact structure and then adds the move Acts leaves out: “called, by those which did not belong to the church … took upon them, gladly, the name of Christ, or Christians, as they were called.” The nickname is accepted. Recover Acts 26:28 — “Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian,” Agrippa's sneer — and 1 Peter 4:16 — “if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed” — and the whole biblical career of the word is a name given from outside and worn under contempt. That is precisely Moroni's argument at 46:18: “we, who are despised because we take upon us the name of Christ.”

46:15.note: The word itself is the evidence. “Christians” is a New Testament coinage that occurs in one KJV verse, and Alma 46:15 uses it in that verse's own frame: a body of believers named by people outside it, the name then owned. The catalogue's exclusion at Alma 23:16 declined Acts 11:26 there because that passage shares nothing but the idea of a distinguishing name; the objection does not apply here, where the shared item is the singular noun. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not a quotation, but the rarity is absolute.

46:17.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

provenance.other: “Poured out his soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 53:12. Luke 22:37 quotes the neighbouring clause of that verse and not this one; mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for the Isaiah form, so the route is direct-OT and the New Testament is not in play.
provenance.significance: The one biblical soul poured out is the servant's, and it is poured out unto death, as the price of interceding for transgressors. Alma 46:17 pours out a soul in prayer for a people about to go to war, and the sentence it opens ends by naming the land “a chosen land, and the land of liberty.” The suppressed correspondence is the cost: in Isaiah the pouring out buys a portion divided with the great, and here it precedes a chapter of executions (46:35) for those who will not covenant. The catalogue does not claim the writer meant the servant song; it records that the phrase available to him for total self-expenditure in prayer was a phrase the KJV uses once, of a death.

46:17.note: “When he had poured out his soul to God.” A four-word KJV singleton, and the Book of Mormon uses it of prayer where Isaiah uses it of dying. That semantic shift is why this is an echo and not an allusion: nothing else in 46:17 touches Isaiah 53, and the phrase may simply have entered the writer's English as a devotional idiom. It is recorded because the idiom has exactly one biblical home.
46:17.whyNot: “Pour out the soul” is close to 1 Samuel 1:15's “poured out my soul before the LORD,” which is prayer and not death and which would make the Book of Mormon's usage unremarkable; the exact string is Isaiah's alone, but the idea is Hannah's.

46:20.text: I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.

provenance.other: “In the strength of the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 71:16 and Micah 5:4. Psalm 71:16 has the verb of motion the Book of Mormon uses (“I will GO in the strength of the Lord GOD”); Micah 5:4's is a verb of standing and feeding.
provenance.significance: The catalogue adjudicated this phrase at Mosiah 9:17, where Zeniff's people go out to battle in it; the link is written afresh here because Alma is a new book with a new narrator's voice and the reader of Alma 46 should not be shown silence. What is new here is the imperative. Psalm 71 is a single old man's confidence — “I will go” — and Moroni turns it into a summons to a nation: “let them come forth in the strength of the Lord.” The Psalm's first person becomes a muster.

46:20.note: “Let them come forth in the strength of the Lord, and enter into a covenant.” Two KJV verses have the phrase and one of them has the Book of Mormon's verb of going. The wording is short enough that a reader could call it common English piety, so it is an echo at moderate confidence; the argument is the same one made at Mosiah 9:17, and is not restated here at length.

46:21.text: Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf.

provenance.other: “Suffer as a Christian” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 4:16, and it is the only place in the Bible where the noun “Christian” and the verb “ashamed” stand together. Alma 46:21 has “be ashamed to take upon them the name of Christ”; 46:18 has “despised because we take upon us the name of Christ.”
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 4:16 is the New Testament's one instruction about how to hold the name under pressure, and it holds it two ways at once: do not be ashamed, and glorify God. Alma 46 splits the verse across its covenant. The people rend their garments as a token that if they are ever “ashamed to take upon them the name of Christ,” the Lord should rend them likewise — Peter's shame clause turned into a self-imprecation. And 46:16, where Moroni prays that the cause of the Christians might be favoured, is Peter's second clause: the name is glorified rather than concealed. The suppressed term is persecution. Peter's Christians suffer from outside; Moroni's covenant makes the danger internal, and the thing to be ashamed of is one's own transgression.

46:21.note: The chapter's three uses of the Christian name (46:15, 46:18, 46:21) exhaust the KJV's three verses containing that noun, and this one takes the rarest pairing in them: shame and the name together, which the King James Bible puts in one verse only. The covenant clause “be ashamed to take upon them the name of Christ” is 1 Peter 4:16's “let him not be ashamed” restated as the condition of a curse. No clause is reproduced verbatim, so this is an allusion, not a quotation, and it is far below Skousen's threshold.

46:21.text: When Jesus saw that the people came running together, he rebuked the foul spirit, saying unto him, Thou dumb and deaf spirit, I charge thee, come out of him, and enter no more into him.

provenance.other: “The people came running together” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 9:25. The five words are reproduced in order and without change.
provenance.significance: Mark 9:25 is a crowd forming around a leader who then acts decisively in front of it, and the King James translators used this phrase nowhere else. Alma 46:21 has the identical five words in the identical function — Moroni proclaims, and the people come running together — but Mark's crowd is a spectacle drawn by a failed exorcism, and Moroni's is a covenant assembly. If the borrowing is real it is a borrowing of narrative furniture rather than of meaning, which is itself worth recording: this catalogue's other Markan links (1 Nephi 7:11's “how great things”) are of the same kind, phrases taken for their usefulness and not their theology.

46:21.note: Five consecutive words, exactly as the KJV has them, from the only verse in the Bible that contains them. Against that, there is no thematic contact whatever with Mark 9 and no other Markan wording in the chapter, so the possibility that two writers independently reached for the natural English of a gathering crowd cannot be dismissed — hence echo at moderate rather than allusion. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold.
46:21.whyNot: “The people came running together” is unremarkable English and the KJV's single occurrence may be an accident of how rarely the KJV describes crowds forming. Nothing else in Alma 46 touches Mark's exorcism, and no argument improves by importing it.

46:22.text: And they brought him to Jesus: and they cast their garments upon the colt, and they set Jesus thereon.

provenance.other: “Cast their garments” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 11:7 and Luke 19:35, both of the triumphal entry; Matthew 21:8 has “spread their garments in the way,” and Luke 19:36 adds “they spread their clothes in the way.” 2 Kings 9:13 is the Old Testament analogue — “they hasted, and took every man his garment, and put it under him on the top of the stairs” — where garments cast down proclaim a king.
provenance.significance: In the King James Bible, casting garments before a man is an act of acclamation and it makes him a king: Jehu on the stairs, Jesus on the colt, in both cases with a crowd shouting. Alma 46:22 stages the gesture and cancels its meaning. The people cast their garments at Moroni's feet, but not to enthrone him — the words spoken over the casting are a curse on themselves, and the garments are cast down “to be trodden under foot” rather than ridden over. The chapter's whole quarrel is with a man who wants to be king (46:4), and this is the one moment where its crowd performs the biblical coronation gesture toward someone who is not going to accept it.

46:22.note: The exact phrase belongs to two verses of the triumphal entry and to no others, and it arrives here in a chapter already dense with New Testament rarities. The sense, however, is inverted: acclamation in Mark and Luke, self-abasement here. Catalogued as an echo because the inversion is complete and three words is a thin base; it is recorded rather than excluded because the inversion is legible as an argument, not as a mismatch.
46:22.whyNot: “Cast their garments” may be nothing more than the ordinary English for the action Alma 46:22 describes, which really does involve garments being thrown down; the two KJV occurrences agree with it in wording and disagree with it in everything else. A reader who requires shared sense as well as shared words should decline this row.

46:23.text: And he knew it, and said, It is my son’s coat; an evil beast hath devoured him; Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces.

provenance.other: “Rent in pieces” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 37:33 — Jacob's cry over the bloodied coat. Alma 46:23 has “whose coat was rent by his brethren, into many pieces.” Note that the Book of Mormon has moved the tearing: in Genesis the brothers dip the coat in blood and do not tear it, and it is Joseph, not the coat, whom Jacob supposes to be rent in pieces.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's hinge, and its interest is in what it gets wrong. Moroni identifies his people as the remnant of Joseph and grounds the identification in a torn coat — but the coat of Genesis 37 was not torn. Jacob's words “rent in pieces” are an inference about his son's body from a garment that has only been bloodied, and Alma 46:23 collapses the inference into the object, so that the brothers tear the coat because Jacob said Joseph was torn. Whether that is a misreading of Genesis or a deliberate fusion of the coat with the extra-biblical remnant tradition Moroni then quotes at 46:24, it is the same operation the chapter has been performing since 46:12: a garment torn by kinsmen becomes a sign that a people can be preserved in pieces. The rest of Moroni's speech — prison, sold, slain (46:23) — is Joseph's biography in three verbs, and the KJV supplies all three in Genesis 37 and 39.
provenance.alternative: Alma 46:24's prophecy of Jacob about the preserved remnant of the coat is not in the King James Bible at all; no source can be assigned to it here, and it is registered as an exclusion rather than forced onto Genesis 37.

46:23.note: Hardy's study edition cross-references Genesis 37:31-33 at this verse, and the wording bears it out: “rent in pieces” is a KJV singleton, and it belongs to the moment Jacob is shown the coat. Moroni's sentence reproduces the two decisive elements — Joseph's coat, and its being rent into pieces — while relocating the tearing from the father's imagination of his son's body to the brothers' hands. The remaining verbs of 46:23, “cast into prison, or be sold, or be slain,” run the rest of the Joseph story forward. It is not a quotation and falls below Skousen's threshold; as an allusion its rarity is absolute.

46:35.text: And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul;

provenance.other: “Entered into a covenant” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 15:12 and Ezekiel 16:8, and only the first has the Book of Mormon's construction with an infinitive of purpose (“to seek the LORD” / “to support the cause of freedom,” “to keep the peace” at 46:31). “Whosoever would not” occurs in exactly two, 2 Chronicles 15:13 and Ezra 10:8, and only the first attaches death to the refusal. The 1830 reads “there was but few which denied the covenant of freedom”, which 1920 corrected to “were … who”.
provenance.significance: Asa's covenant at Jerusalem is the King James Bible's one national oath enforced by execution, and Alma 46 rebuilds it clause by clause. Both begin with a purge of dissenters and a gathering (2 Chronicles 15:8-10 / Alma 46:28); both have a people entering into a covenant with a stated object; both provide that whosoever would not enter it should be put to death (15:13 / 46:35); both swear it with a loud voice and shouting (15:14 / Alma 46:19-21); and both end in rest and peace given to the land (15:15, “the LORD gave them rest round about” / Alma 46:37, “they began to have peace again in the land”). Recover the Chronicler's context and the most uncomfortable sentence in Alma 46 stops being an outlier: Moroni executing the men who would not covenant is Asa's covenant clause carried out, and the Book of Mormon has kept the biblical penalty while changing what is sworn to from the God of Israel to a free government. The substitution is the finding. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the suppressed term here is that in Chronicles the covenant is religious and the death penalty is for apostasy, and Alma 46 has transposed both onto a constitution.

46:35.note: “Whomsoever of the Amalickiahites that would not enter into a covenant to support the cause of freedom, that they might maintain a free government, he caused to be put to death.” Two rare KJV constructions meet in this sentence — the covenant entered into with an infinitive of purpose, and the “whosoever would not” whose penalty is death — and both belong to one biblical passage, Asa's covenant assembly in 2 Chronicles 15:12-13. The correspondence extends past the wording to the sequence of the whole chapter, which is why this is catalogued as structural. No clause is reproduced verbatim and it falls below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; the evidence is the co-occurrence of two two-verse rarities in the same syntactic frame.
46:35.whyNot: “Enter into a covenant” is one of the Book of Mormon's own standing formulas and appears four times in this chapter alone, so its KJV rarity may reflect the King James translators' idiom rather than a borrowing; and a leader executing men who refuse an oath is a situation that can be invented without a model. The structural argument is what carries the row, and structural arguments are the easiest to construct after the fact.
